extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and epistemology; scientists interested in the theory of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for judging the credibility of asserted facts, the limits and application of mathematical/deductive methods, and when to believe, disbelieve, or suspend judgment. Targets evaluation of testimony, induction, causal laws, and anomalous claims (e.g., miracles, novel kinds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstration is purely deductive
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrating an algebraical theorem, or in resolving an equation, we travel from the datum to the quæsitum by pure ratiocination; the only premises introduced, besides the original hypotheses, are the fundamental axioms (e.g., that things equal to the same thing are equal, and that sums of equals are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each step apply one or other of these truths or truths deducible from them; the processes of algebra and higher mathematics are deductive rather than inductive. Use only original hypotheses and acknowledged axioms as premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraical notation for general reasoning on functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraical notation provides a nomenclature enabling us to express numbers generically so as to show what function each is of the other (e.g., expressions a and a^2+3a denote any number and the number formed from it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ symbolic expressions to state general problems (e.g., expressing F as a function of x and then asking what F will be of any function of x), thereby making modes of formation explicit and enabling general theorems (e.g., binomial theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry's axioms and definitions as premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry rests on a small number of general principles: (1) sums of equals are equal; (2) things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; (3) magnitudes which can be applied to coincide are equal. Definitions assert the existence of geometrical objects and at least one property of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these axioms and definitions as the ultimate premises from which geometric theorems are deductively derived; recognize that assumptions (e.g., existence of straight lines, circles, parallel lines) are foundational and not further proved within the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on applicability of mathematical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical principles are inapplicable where causes are so imperfectly accessible that numerical laws cannot be ascertained by proper induction, where causes are numerous/complex that computation transcends calculus powers, or where causes fluctuate (e.g., physiology, social sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying mathematical models check whether (a) underlying causes can be observed and their numerical laws induced, (b) the aggregate effect is computable with available methods, and (c) causes are stable enough. If not, mathematical accuracy may come 'at the expense of the reality of the inquiry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mathematical training as training in deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical training is chiefly valuable not for specific doctrines but as the most perfect type of the Deductive Method, teaching how to employ laws of simpler phenomena to explain/predict those of the complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mathematics primarily as a methodological school for scientific reasoning rather than expecting blanket applicability across complex empirical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disbelief (as positive conviction of falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: By disbelief is meant not mere absence of belief but the state in which we are fully persuaded that some opinion is not true, so that even strong apparent evidence would be judged false or mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between failing to believe for lack of evidence and actively disbelieving because the claim conflicts with stronger inductive grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility vs improbability (criterion for disbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact is impossible when it contradicts a completed induction (a law of nature established by rigorous induction); it is improbable when it conflicts only with approximate generalizations and thus may be provisionally disbelieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the opposing generalization is 'complete' (rigorous induction) or merely approximate; if complete, the alleged fact should be disbelieved unless evidence equivalent to that which established the law is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentum crucis for establishing causal law
rubrics_metrics.description: If antecedent A, superadded to various sets of antecedents, is repeatedly followed by effect B (including trials with many different antecedents), then A can be regarded as the whole cause of B and thus a law; any assertion that A occurred without B (in absence of counteracting cause) must be disbelieved unless equivalent evidence is provided to overturn the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require evidence of the same calibre that established a law (repeated, varied, independently observed experiments) to accept a contradiction to that law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle as introduction of a new cause (how to treat miraculous claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction to the law of cause and effect but a new effect produced by introduction of a new cause (e.g., an act of will by a being with power over nature); to judge it one must compare hypotheses: supernatural agency vs unknown natural cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who do not already believe in supernatural agencies cannot be convinced by a miracle; those who do must weigh conformity of the event to the supposed agent's character and consider antecedent improbability that such an agency acted in that instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess testimony vs established generalizations by comparing approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where positive evidence (testimony/perception) conflicts with generalizations, the decision depends on which set of approximate generalizations (supporting the affirmative or the negative) is stronger or closer to universality; if the negative generalizations are stronger, disbelieve provisionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate the relative strength of underlying generalizations; prefer the side supported by more universal/rigorous induction unless the testimony's evidence is equally strong and capable of overturning the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of alleged new Kinds (conflict with uniformities of co-existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alleged fact would establish a new Kind (a property or species previously unknown), it is not inherently incredible and usually merits suspension of judgment pending confirmation—unless it contradicts known properties of a larger kind which include it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assertions come from unexplored regions and do not violate broader, well-established generalizations, withhold judgment and seek independent confirmation; if the asserted properties violate fundamentals of a larger kind, treat the claim as highly improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate antecedent improbability via knowledge of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion that a cause existed without its usual effect should be disbelieved or not according as it is probable that an adequate counteracting cause was present; form the estimate based on previous knowledge of frequency or rarity of such counteracting causes and whether they would have left other marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior frequency data and consideration of whether such a cause would have manifested itself elsewhere; judge whether error/mendacity in witnesses is more or less probable than the presence of a hidden counteracting cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of judgment is the prudent default for anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where neither the evidence for an alleged anomaly nor the antecedent improbability decisively outweighs the other, a cautious person should neither admit nor reject the testimony but wait for confirmation from other, unconnected sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt suspension pending additional observations unless the testimony is free from suspicious circumstances and independent confirmations accumulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sift testimony for fallacies, delusions, and motives undermining credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonial reports that later proved false often contained circumstances (fallacious appearances, epidemic delusion, strong interests—religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, or passion for the marvelous) that would, on careful sifting, have rendered the testimony untrustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively search for signs of sensory error, mass delusion, vested interests, emotional bias, or other motives that would explain the reported impression without accepting the fact as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish improbability before the fact from improbability after it
rubrics_metrics.description: Many events are improbable before they occur (e.g., a particular face on a die) but are not incredible after being reported by credible witnesses, provided the fact is not contrary to any approximate induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing an event merely because it was unlikely beforehand; evaluate it in light of whether its occurrence is incompatible with established generalizations and on the credibility of the evidence presented (example: ace on a die — improbable before, credible after suitable testimony).
